title: Hull Structural Integrity Inspection Ghent | Canal Port Ships
description: Hull structural integrity inspection at Ghent: corrosion pattern, grab damage, lock contact deformation and crack checks on bulkers, ro-ro and cargo ships.
h1: Structural Condition Assessment of Hulls Calling at the Port of Ghent
intro: A hull that works the Ghent canal trade takes damage from three directions at once: abrasive and corrosive cargo in the holds, repeated contact with quays and lock fendering on the passage from Terneuzen, and ordinary fatigue at the structural details that always crack first. Atlantis NDT assesses that condition by combining ultrasonic thickness gauging with a record of pitting, grooving, deformation and magnetic particle crack checks, so the owner and the attending surveyor see the pattern behind the numbers. Our technicians travel from India to the ship at the berth.

highlights.h: Cargo damage and canal contact together
highlights.p: Ships here accumulate grab impact in the holds and scrapes along the shell from lock and quay contact. The assessment records both, because a dented plate that is also wasted behaves differently from one that is merely thin.

General thinning, pitting, grooving at weld lines and edge corrosion each call for a different repair. The report names the pattern at every measured location instead of leaving the reader to infer it from a column of readings.

highlights.h: Fatigue details checked on the same visit
highlights.p: Hatch corners, bracket toes, ramp hinges and crane foundations are examined by magnetic particle testing while the team is aboard, so cracks and wastage are found in one attendance rather than two.

sections.h: Where can a hull structural assessment be carried out in Ghent?
p: The assessment follows the ship's own routine at the berth. At the steelworks quays, bulk carriers are inspected once discharge ends: holds can be lit and staged, and the sides, frames and tank tops are accessible for a close look. At agribulk and forest-product berths the holds are cleaner, which lets the team examine coatings and plating without a layer of cargo residue, and the weather decks and coamings are reachable from the quay side.

Ro-ro ships and vehicle carriers are examined during rotation gaps, with car decks, ramps and lashing points accessible once the vehicles have gone. The tank terminals along the canal host tankers whose deck structure and exposed ballast tank boundaries can be assessed alongside, while the cargo tanks wait for a gas-free certificate.

A dry hull is not available here for deep-sea ships, so the underwater shell is left for a docking elsewhere. What Ghent allows is the whole above-water structure, the holds and any tank the crew can ventilate, which is where most of the structural judgement for bulk carriers is made anyway.
list: Holds, hoppers and topside tanks of bulk carriers after discharge
Weather deck, coamings and hatch corners at any cargo berth
Car decks, ramps and ramp hinges on ro-ro ships between rotations
Deck structure and ballast boundaries on tankers at the canal terminals

sections.h: Which ships at Ghent need a structural integrity assessment, and when?
p: The usual trigger is age combined with trade. A bulk carrier approaching its second or third renewal survey after years of ore and coal needs to know whether the hold frames are healthy before the yard is booked. A buyer inspecting a handysize bulker at an agribulk berth wants the same answer before the sale closes, with no wish to discover wasted steel after delivery.

Charterers and technical managers also ask for assessments after an incident: a hard contact in the lock, a grab dropped on a tank top, or a heavy-weather passage reported by the master. These events produce local deformation that needs a measured record, since a surveyor will ask whether the plating is still within its margins.

Port state control is another reason. Under the Paris MoU a bulk carrier of a certain age and profile can be selected for a more detailed inspection, and holds are easy for an inspector to examine. An owner who arrives with a current structural record and documented repairs is in a stronger position than one who relies on visual impressions.

sections.h: How is the assessment scoped for a canal-trade hull?
p: Scoping starts with the ship's own history: the last thickness measurement report, the survey status, the cargo trade and any damage reports. From these the team builds a list of structure to examine and gauge, grouped by area: the holds, the weather deck and coamings, ballast tanks, the shell above the waterline and, for ro-ro ships, the ramps and car decks.

Gauging follows the thickness measurement plan, but the visual record is as important as the readings. The technician notes coating condition, the form of corrosion, the presence of pitting or grooving, deformation of plating and stiffeners, and any cracks found. Where a plate looks buckled or dented, its flatness is recorded and the surrounding readings are densified so that the extent of damage is defined.

Magnetic particle testing is added at the details that fatigue most often: corners of hatch openings, toes of brackets, crane pedestal welds and the hinges and stoppers of ramps. Surface preparation is arranged with the crew and the yard, and the work is sequenced around hot work, cargo operations and any rain.

sections.h: What do structural assessments typically find on these ships?
p: In holds the dominant finding is wastage of frames and brackets at the lower levels, accompanied by mechanical damage from grabs that bends or tears flanges. Coal trades add corrosion on plating behind the frames. Tank tops are commonly pitted, and where pitting is dense the assessment records its depth and distribution, because scattered shallow pits and a cluster of deep ones lead to different decisions.

In ballast tanks the typical picture is coating failure at the upper corners and along the weld seams, producing grooving that is easy to miss visually. On the shell above the waterline, contact with lock walls leaves local dents and sometimes buckled plating with associated stiffener distortion, and the readings around these areas show whether steel has been lost as well as deformed.

Ro-ro ships show cracking and wear at ramp hinges and at the lower corners of car-deck openings, along with corrosion at drainage areas where water remains. Each finding is reported by location, with the physical condition separated from the gauging result, so a repair specification can address cause as well as symptom.

sections.h: How do you plan a structural assessment around a Ghent call?
p: Plan around the canal timetable. The ship's time at the berth depends on lock slots and the cargo plan, and the assessment needs a known window with the holds empty and access arranged. Send us the expected discharge end, the sailing time and the spaces that can be entered, and the team will rank the areas so the most informative ones are done first.

Share previous survey reports and any damage or repair history. If the purpose is a sale, tell us whether the buyer's surveyor will attend. If the purpose is a class survey in preparation, say which survey and whether a docking is booked, so the findings can be arranged to support it. Visa processing for the team travelling from India begins once the call is confirmed.
Ahead of boarding the ship's agent arranges gate passes, and the master confirms lighting, staging and safe access. Anything not accessible is listed in the report as outstanding.

sections.h: What does a scope look like for a ro-ro ship and a bulker?
p: For a ro-ro ship on a Scandinavian rotation, the work covers main-deck plating, ramp structure, lower car-deck stiffening and the shell sides above the waterline, with magnetic particle testing at ramp hinges and stoppers. The report separates corrosion at drainage areas from wear at moving parts.

For a bulk carrier at the steelworks quay, the scope centres on all holds: frames and brackets, hopper plating, tank tops and coamings, with topside tanks added if they can be emptied. Deformation from grab damage is mapped, and each hold receives a summary of wastage pattern and cracks.

faqs.q: What does a hull structural integrity inspection include at Ghent?
faqs.a: Ultrasonic thickness gauging of accessible structure, a visual record of corrosion form, deformation and coating state, and magnetic particle checks at fatigue-prone details. The scope is set from the ship's survey history and what the crew can make accessible during the call.

faqs.q: Can lock or quay contact damage be assessed at the berth?
faqs.a: Yes, above the waterline. The team records the extent of dents and buckled plating, measures the plate around them, and reports whether steel has been lost as well as deformed. Underwater damage needs a dry hull, so it waits for a docking.

faqs.q: Is this assessment useful before buying a bulk carrier at Ghent?
faqs.a: It is a common use. Hold frames, hopper plating, tank tops and coamings are measured and the pattern of wastage and any cracks recorded, so a buyer sees the real condition of the structure before the sale is concluded.

faqs.q: How are cracks at hatch corners and ramp hinges found?
faqs.a: By magnetic particle testing on cleaned steel at the known details. Indications are measured and photographed on the part. The result is an NDT record for the owner and yard, and the attending surveyor decides what the class requires.

faqs.q: What should we send before the team travels from India to Ghent?
faqs.a: Vessel name or IMO number, ship type, class, trade, previous thickness measurement and survey reports, any damage history, and the expected discharge end and sailing time. With these we shape the scope and start visa processing once you confirm the call.
